title: How to talk to statues — Joe Reeve, ElevenLabs

primary.label: Multimodal & Realtime Systems
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 55%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on realtime voice interaction systems including a statue-talking pipeline, voice design APIs, interruption handling, and embodied physical voice installations. The app creates interactive cultural experiences for museums and public installations, while the voice interaction patterns and vibe coding discussion apply broadly. The statue app is a viral prototype with active discussion of production deployment challenges for cultural institutions including curator interfaces and embedded hardware. Accessible vibe coding concepts are paired with intermediate voice systems engineering such as transcript-based interruption handling and push-to-talk alternatives. A conference presentation featuring a demo video followed by extended audience Q&A on voice interface design and technical challenges. All supporting evidence is drawn directly from statements in the transcript with no external verification.

summary:
Joe Reeve, in the growth organization at ElevenLabs, presents his viral "talk to a statue" app. The pipeline: a user photographs a statue, OpenAI deep research identifies it and generates historical context plus voice description, the ElevenLabs voice design API creates a matching voice, an agent spins up, and conversation begins — all in about 30 seconds. Joe built this in Cursor in two hours on a Sunday with a single one-shot prompt, demoed at the British Museum. The app went viral in two stages: 50K impressions on Tuesday, then 1.5M after a vibe coding repost. Outreach came from museums, auction houses (Bonhams, Christie's), and travel platforms. A museum CEO tracked down Joe's WhatsApp, saying he had 10 people working on similar functionality for a year.

Joe met with the Science Museum co-CEO, who is asking the same questions without clear answers. Current museum tech like tablets can feel tacked on. Joe's team is commissioning a statue with embedded technology (speaker, microphone) so visitors talk directly without a screen intermediary. A red phone booth installation lets visitors pick up a phone and talk to an agent as Sir Michael Caine. The ElevenLabs agents platform supports knowledge files and MCP calling rather than a "skills" concept; people have built phone-based OpenClaw setups that call users back.

On vibe coding, Joe notes events feel like OG hackathons — attendees sometimes don't know apps are made by people. He awaits a "TikTok moment" for social vibe coding. Joe shares a Facebook Instant Games API story: he bought a Fruit Ninja clone for £15, instrumented it with the social/ads API, and woke up to 15 million users in Vietnam. That social-sharing template may be the winning pattern for social vibe coding.

Discussion covers voice output limitations: information density per second is lower than text or diagrams. Some want voice input with information-rich visual output — parallel modalities. The group explores "skim listening" — scrolling forward in concepts rather than sentences, like an iPod scroll wheel. Interruption is a key problem: people are too polite to interrupt voice agents, and agents can't sense listener cues like nodding or "uh-huh." Push-to-talk (hold to talk, release to finish) is proposed as a reliable alternative. A visual "nudge" interface on top of audio could signal when an agent wants to ask a question, showing the topic it wants to discuss. Technically, handling interruptions could involve editing the transcript retroactively using audio timestamps to forget text generated after the interruption point, rather than appending the user's message to the end. The Claude app is noted for showing higher-level sections while speaking, letting users tap to expand.

Joe shares his video creation approach: he learned editing through politics-related campaigning, edited the statue video on his phone in CapCut in about 20-25 minutes using a borrowed DJI Bluetooth lapel mic (£200). Key tips: add captions, front-load the hook (his videos get 6-12 second median view times), and use music — he chose the statue app's "imperial" music before making the video, and uses ElevenLabs music generation to experiment with genres. He recorded the British Museum video twice — the first attempt was boring, so he returned with better city photos.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Intro and ElevenLabs Overview
sections.summary: Joe introduces himself as working in the growth organization at ElevenLabs, then gives an overview of ElevenLabs as an audio AI foundation model company covering text-to-speech, transcription, commercially licensed AI music, sound effects, voice creation/editing, and a managed agents platform. He highlights voice creation as underutilized, especially at hackathons.

sections.title: Statue App Demo and Viral Story
sections.summary: Joe plays a demo video filmed at the British Museum showing conversations with various statues. He explains the pipeline: photo, OpenAI deep research for identification and historical context, ElevenLabs voice design API for matching voice, agent creation, and conversation start — all in 30 seconds. He built it in Cursor in two hours with a one-shot prompt, posted it Tuesday for 50K impressions, reposted about vibe coding for 1.5M. Museums, auction houses, and a museum CEO with a 10-person team all reached out. This led to something called 11 Hacks.

sections.title: Scaling and Production Q&A
sections.summary: Audience asks about scaling. Joe says the app relies on APIs designed to scale, so infrastructure is handled by providers. Vibe coding shows that glue and storytelling matter more than hard technical problems. For production, the real challenge is working with curators to design proper narratives rather than random web research. Museums like the V&A have public collection APIs. No curator interface is designed yet; at best they could edit system prompts in the ElevenLabs dashboard.

sections.title: Voice Interface Design Discussion
sections.summary: Joe discusses voice design philosophy with Jago (formerly British Museum, now Sainsbury Centre), who is exploring what inanimate objects should sound like based on material origins and history. Joe sees opportunity to give voices to everyday objects like elevators. Current voice interface problems include the binary choice between voice and other interaction, the lack of generative UI plus voice hybrids, and the gap between what users talk to and what performs the work.

sections.title: Skills, MCP, and Multimodal Interaction
sections.summary: Joe discusses multimodal conversations combining voice and visual. People are too polite to interrupt voice agents, which degrades the experience. On skills for agents: the ElevenLabs platform doesn't support a skills concept per se but does support knowledge files and MCP calling for embedding capabilities. People have built phone-based OpenClaw setups where agents call users back, and voice capabilities can be added to existing coding agents.

sections.title: Museum Innovation and Embedded Technology
sections.summary: Joe met with the co-CEO of the Science Museum, who is asking the same questions without clear answers. Existing museum tech like tablets can feel tacked on. Joe's team is commissioning a statue with embedded technology (speaker, microphone) so visitors talk directly without a screen. A red phone booth installation lets visitors pick up a phone and talk to an agent as Sir Michael Caine, putting the experience into the physical world rather than through a screen.

sections.title: Vibe Coding Events and Consumer Mainstream
sections.summary: Joe describes vibe coding events as feeling like OG hackathons — attendees sometimes don't even know apps are made by people. Non-coders describe desired UI without knowing terms like hamburger menu or accordion, producing unexpected results because the LLM just tries it. Joe awaits an Instagram-filters or TikTok moment for social vibe coding. Spielwork is a mobile app for vibe coding games with TikTok swiping; a London-based game vibe coding tool exists too, but Joe thinks most efforts are just lovable-on-mobile rather than pushing boundaries.

sections.title: Facebook Instant Games and Social Vibe Coding
sections.summary: Joe shares that the Facebook Instant Games API — now deprecated — is the closest pattern to a winner for social vibe coding. It provided primitives for social gaming: user info, friends, leaderboards, key-value storage, and ads. Joe bought a Fruit Ninja clone for £15, instrumented it with the API, went to bed, and woke up with 15 million users in Vietnam because Facebook tests in lower-value advertising regions. The social sharing element is key to the template.

sections.title: Voice Output Density and Interaction Patterns
sections.summary: An audience member raises frustration with voice output: information density per second isn't high enough. They want voice input with information-rich visual output (diagrams, text, UI) — parallel input/output but single voice input. Another notes voice provides companionship and motivation beyond raw information. The visual cortex is older than voice and text. Concise answers feel rude in speech but acceptable in text. The group wonders what skim listening with forward/back controls would look like.

sections.title: Skim Listening and Interruption Solutions
sections.summary: The group elaborates on skim listening — wanting to scroll forward in concepts, not sentences, like an iPod scroll wheel or podcast 2x speed. The interruption problem is explored further: agents can't sense listener cues like nodding or 'uh-huh,' users don't know how long a response will be, and saying 'be concise' produces rude-sounding output. The Claude app is noted for showing higher-level sections while speaking with tappable expand. An audience member describes PS5 game work (at 'How I Met Joe') where voice creates in-game objects, using push-to-talk (hold to talk, release to finish) as a reliable alternative to pure voice interruptibility. A visual 'nudge' interface is proposed — showing when an agent wants to ask a question and signaling the topic, avoiding unwanted interruption.

sections.title: Technical Handling of Interruptions and Transcript Editing
sections.summary: Technical discussion covers how to handle agent interruptions. Current agent platforms generate full text then audio and append interrupted messages to the end. Joe proposes using audio timestamps to edit the transcript retroactively — since we know how far through the audio has played, we can forget text generated after the interruption point. An asynchronous approach of repeatedly analyzing the transcript for whether the agent has something to add is also discussed, rather than relying on tool calls. Joe invites the audience to vibe code at the ElevenLabs booth.

sections.title: Video Creation Approach and Tips
sections.summary: Joe shares his video creation process. He learned editing through politics-related campaigning before joining ElevenLabs. The statue video was edited on his phone in CapCut in about 20-25 minutes using a borrowed DJI Bluetooth lapel mic (£200). Key tips: add captions, front-load the hook (his videos get 6-12 second median view times before drop-off), and use music — he chose the statue app's 'imperial' music before making the video, and uses ElevenLabs music generation to experiment with different genres. He recorded the British Museum video twice — the first attempt was boring, so he returned with better city photos. Desktop editing (even CapCut on desktop) is three times harder and more expensive than mobile.
